extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors (especially debut authors) participating in Twitter pitch contests (PitMad, DVPit, etc.)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for drafting a concise, agent-attracting Twitter pitch for book manuscripts to use in pitch contests; covers content, tone, hashtags, etiquette, and when a manuscript may not suit a 280-character pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow contest rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Each event has its own rules about when it is scheduled, how often you can pitch, and how many projects you can pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the event website and follow and respect the rules for every contest—you don’t want to make a bad impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform etiquette and visibility mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Please refrain from liking your friends’ pitches and show support by retweeting or commenting, because too many likes will make the results confusing to sort through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that participating agents read feeds and 'like' pitches that catch their eye; likes indicate interest and too many likes can obscure real signals. Support peers with retweets/comments rather than mass likes so results remain clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet agents and follow querying instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating agents will post instructions on their feeds about how to query them if they like your pitch. Remember, you don’t have to submit to everyone who requests. Carefully vet the agents and editors you submit to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agent requests more, check their preferences and submission requirements before querying; prioritize agents who are a good fit rather than sending to everyone who expresses interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core pitch formula (goal + obstacle + action)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, lay out in plain terms what your main character wants, what stands in their way, and what they need to do to get it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the statement short and simple; explicitly state the protagonist's desire, the central obstacle/conflict, and the action they must take. Example: 'Ex-FBI agent Tonya must rescue her kidnapped son from her ex-husband by facing down his dangerous biker gang.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision and careful word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep it short and simple. Pick words carefully to convey the stakes of the story and the relationships between key characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to communicate the essence within Twitter’s length constraints (reduce to ~280 characters). Use precise, evocative language that signals stakes, tone, and relationships without extra exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal genre, setting, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without tags, we should catch hints of genre, setting, and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words and details that line up with genre expectations so agents scanning for specific categories will notice (e.g., 'hardened soldier', 'witch princess', 'Bathtub of Doom').

rubrics_metrics.name: Show conflict and dramatic tension aligned with genre
rubrics_metrics.description: These pitches [...] all clearly indicate conflict and dramatic tension, with themes that line up well with their respective genres. Agents reading these pitches and looking for these genres will take notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the pitch foregrounds the central conflict and stakes so it reads as a compelling, genre-appropriate logline rather than just a premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add a hook or twist (high-concept distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the pitch up a notch by adding a hook or twist to show off the high-concept nature of the manuscript we’re pitching. What sets it apart on the market? How might it subvert our expectations or add a deeper layer of conflict?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapose a surprising twist against the established premise to demonstrate that the book fits a category while offering something new. Examples: append twist clauses such as '—only to discover her preteen may have masterminded his own abduction' or 'Her enchanted mask ... slowly consuming her own identity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include comp titles and proper hashtags; categorize by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have the body of your pitch, add details, comp titles and the proper hashtags. Don’t forget to categorize your pitch by genre—agents use these to search Twitter feeds for the genres they represent!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format comps and tags clearly (e.g., 'BABY TEETH + SONS OF ANARCHY' followed by '#PitCon #A #T' or '#PitCon #YA #F'). Use event tags and genre abbreviations so agents can filter and find your pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when a manuscript is not suitable for a Twitter pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all books can or should be reduced to a Twitter pitch. Stories where the language is the selling point, with multiple main characters and plotlines, or stories with complicated worldbuilding, can be difficult to communicate in 280 characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your novel’s strengths are literary language, multiple POVs, or intricate worldbuilding, consider other submission routes rather than forcing a reductive pitch that misrepresents the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pitch as a diagnostic tool for manuscript clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: For debut authors, crafting a Twitter pitch can be an excellent way to ... identify strengths and weaknesses in your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you struggle to identify stakes or a high-concept angle, ask what characters stand to lose if they fail, and what makes the book feel fresh in its genre. Use difficulties in pitching as signals of where the manuscript may need sharpening.
